doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

chapter: Back to Chicago and the road to jail and illness
title: Musicians once helped each other
summary: Ware reflects on how musicians helped one another in the fifties, with a note on Marvin Gaye.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Yeah ... to straighten me out, you know. Then he took me over to the side and he says you shouldn't be staying there; you should have a place here on the south side, so the cats can get to you more readily and you'd be able to go out and play more, you know.

And he did all that just because I helped him once, and actually, that's what some of the musicians are about. At one time, they used to help each other, you know? Like in the fifties, the guys that weren't working this week, they'd come to their jobs and they knew if they played right, and they asked you to help them, you did what you could. And the same way when you was uptight, and you'd go down to his job on his pay nights, and he'd help you.
Of course it doesn't happen like that no more; when these guys see you now they sneak off, you know.
Like the thing that was in the paper recently where the guys were awarded money for not getting paid at all ... like Marvin Gaye.
Oh, that was something. Wasn't that somethin'? Here the guy worked and Marvin Gaye took him to court, civil court to get his money.
